config.title: Rate limiting at scale

intro.title: Rate limiting at scale
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple rate limiter to control how many requests a server accepts from a client over a set time window. You'll learn the core concept of a token bucket algorithm, which is a common method for managing traffic flow and preventing system overload. The main constructs involved are counters, timestamps, and conditional logic to check request limits. This hands-on exercise will help you understand how large-scale applications maintain stability and fairness under heavy user traffic.
intro.usecase: Rate limiting is essential for protecting APIs and services from abuse or overload in production systems. You'll implement it when building public APIs like those from Twitter or Stripe, where you need to control request volumes per user or IP. This pattern appears in cloud dashboards showing usage quotas, e-commerce checkout flows preventing bot purchases, and streaming services managing concurrent connections. As a developer, you'll configure rate limits to ensure fair usage, prevent DDoS attacks, and maintain system stability under high traffic.

objectives: Implement a token bucket algorithm for rate limiting
Configure rate limit parameters for different API endpoints
Integrate rate limiting middleware into a distributed system
Construct a sliding window log to track request timestamps
Apply rate limiting strategies to handle burst traffic
Initialize a rate limiter with capacity and refill rate settings
Manipulate request counters based on client identifiers

steps.title: Define the core rate limiting concepts and requirements
steps.instruction: Create a function named defineRateLimiting that returns a string describing what rate limiting is, why it's needed at scale, and the key requirements.
steps.hint: The function should return a single string that explains the concept. You can write it as a multi-line string or a single concatenated string.
steps.expectedOutcome: A function named defineRateLimiting that returns a descriptive string about rate limiting concepts.
successCriteria: The defineRateLimiting function exists and returns a string containing explanations of rate limiting, its need at scale, and key requirements.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the function that defines the core concepts of rate limiting.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've created a function, but make sure it returns a string describing rate limiting concepts and requirements.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function is missing or doesn't return the required descriptive string about rate limiting.

steps.title: Identify the rate limiting algorithm options
steps.instruction: Inside your defineRateLimiting function, create a list of common rate limiting algorithm names as strings.
steps.hint: You can create an array of algorithm names like 'Token Bucket', 'Leaky Bucket', etc.
steps.expectedOutcome: The function should return an array containing the names of common rate limiting algorithms.
successCriteria: The defineRateLimiting function returns an array with at least 3 algorithm names.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully listed the common rate limiting algorithms. This is the foundation for comparing their scalability characteristics.
steps.feedbackPartial: You have some algorithm names, but try to include more common ones like Token Bucket, Leaky Bucket, and Fixed Window Counter.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function doesn't return an array of algorithm names. Remember to create an array with string values representing different rate limiting algorithms.

steps.title: Choose the sliding window counter algorithm for this design
steps.instruction: Inside your defineRateLimiting function, add a comment explaining why you're selecting the sliding window counter algorithm for this design.
steps.hint: Add a single-line or multi-line comment that mentions the algorithm's balance between accuracy and scalability.
steps.expectedOutcome: The defineRateLimiting function now contains a comment explaining the algorithm selection.
successCriteria: A comment exists inside defineRateLimiting that mentions selecting the sliding window counter algorithm and references accuracy and scalability.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've documented your algorithm selection with clear reasoning about accuracy and scalability.
steps.feedbackPartial: You added a comment, but make sure it explicitly mentions selecting the sliding window counter algorithm and references both accuracy and scalability.
steps.feedbackWrong: The comment should explain why you're choosing the sliding window counter algorithm, mentioning its balance between accuracy and scalability for large-scale systems.

steps.title: Design the data storage strategy for distributed systems
steps.instruction: Inside the defineRateLimiting function, add a comment describing the need for Redis or a similar in-memory data store with atomic operations to handle concurrent requests across multiple servers.
steps.hint: Focus on explaining why distributed systems require a shared storage solution with atomic operations for consistency.
steps.expectedOutcome: The function includes a clear comment about using Redis or similar in-memory store with atomic operations for distributed rate limiting.
successCriteria: A comment exists inside defineRateLimiting describing Redis/in-memory store with atomic operations for distributed concurrent requests.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've correctly identified the storage requirement for distributed rate limiting systems.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your comment specifically mentions Redis/in-memory store and atomic operations for handling concurrent requests.
steps.feedbackWrong: The comment should describe using Redis or similar in-memory data store with atomic operations to handle concurrent requests across multiple servers.

steps.title: Define the rate limiting key structure
steps.instruction: Inside the defineRateLimiting function, create a function named generateRateLimitKey that takes two parameters: scope and identifier, and returns a string in the format 'ratelimit:{scope}:{identifier}'.
steps.hint: Think about how to construct a unique key string by combining the scope and identifier with a consistent prefix and separator.
steps.expectedOutcome: The defineRateLimiting function now contains a generateRateLimitKey function that returns properly formatted rate limiting keys.
successCriteria: The generateRateLimitKey function exists inside defineRateLimiting, takes two parameters, and returns a string in the format 'ratelimit:{scope}:{identifier}'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully defined the key structure function. This will allow us to create unique identifiers for different rate limiting scopes like user, IP, or API key.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your function returns a string in the exact format 'ratelimit:{scope}:{identifier}' and accepts both scope and identifier parameters.
steps.feedbackWrong: The key structure function isn't quite right. Remember to create a function that takes scope and identifier parameters and returns a formatted string with the 'ratelimit:' prefix.

steps.title: Design the sliding window counter implementation logic
steps.instruction: Inside the defineRateLimiting function, create a function named slidingWindowCounter that takes parameters for key, currentTimestamp, windowSizeInSeconds, and maxRequests.
steps.hint: This function will implement the sliding window algorithm logic. Start by declaring the function with the specified parameters.
steps.expectedOutcome: A slidingWindowCounter function is defined with the required parameters, ready for algorithm implementation.
successCriteria: The slidingWindowCounter function exists with parameters key, currentTimestamp, windowSizeInSeconds, and maxRequests.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've created the slidingWindowCounter function with the correct parameters. This will serve as the foundation for implementing the sliding window algorithm logic.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've created a function, but it's missing some required parameters. Make sure to include key, currentTimestamp, windowSizeInSeconds, and maxRequests as parameters.
steps.feedbackWrong: The slidingWindowCounter function is not properly defined. Create a function with the specified parameters inside defineRateLimiting.

steps.title: Add burst handling and smooth rate limiting
steps.instruction: Inside the slidingWindowCounter function, add logic to allow a burst capacity of up to 2 requests while ensuring the average rate doesn't exceed 10 requests per minute over the sliding window period.
steps.hint: You can implement burst handling by temporarily allowing a higher request count at the start of the window, then gradually reducing the available capacity as time passes within the window.
steps.expectedOutcome: The slidingWindowCounter function now includes burst handling logic that allows temporary bursts while maintaining the overall rate limit over the sliding window period.
successCriteria: The slidingWindowCounter function contains burst capacity logic with calculations for effective maximum requests based on elapsed time in the window.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully implemented burst handling in your rate limiter. This allows temporary request bursts while ensuring the overall rate limit is maintained over the sliding window period.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added some burst handling logic, but it might not fully implement the gradual reduction of burst capacity over time. Check that your calculation accounts for elapsed time in the window.
steps.feedbackWrong: The burst handling logic appears to be missing or incorrect. Remember to implement logic that allows a burst capacity at the start of the window that gradually reduces as time passes within the window.

steps.title: Design the distributed coordination mechanism
steps.instruction: Add a function named 'distributedCoordination' inside the defineRateLimiting function that uses Redis transactions or Lua scripts to ensure atomic operations when multiple servers check/update the same rate limit counter.
steps.hint: Create a function that handles the atomic update logic needed for distributed coordination. Focus on the concept of ensuring consistency across multiple instances.
steps.expectedOutcome: The defineRateLimiting function now includes a distributedCoordination function that addresses atomic operations for distributed rate limiting.
successCriteria: A function named 'distributedCoordination' is defined inside defineRateLimiting and references Redis transactions or Lua scripts for atomic operations.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added the distributed coordination mechanism that ensures consistency across multiple rate limiter instances.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added a function, but make sure it's named 'distributedCoordination' and references atomic operations using Redis transactions or Lua scripts.
steps.feedbackWrong: The distributed coordination function is missing or incorrectly named. Create a function named 'distributedCoordination' inside defineRateLimiting that handles atomic operations.

steps.title: Add response headers and client communication
steps.instruction: Inside your defineRateLimiting function, add a new function named addRateLimitHeaders that returns an object with the headers X-RateLimit-Limit, X-RateLimit-Remaining, X-RateLimit-Reset, and a status property.
steps.hint: Create a function that returns an object with the required header keys and example values.
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have a function that returns the rate limit headers object, ready to be used in API responses.
successCriteria: The addRateLimitHeaders function exists inside defineRateLimiting and returns an object with X-RateLimit-Limit, X-RateLimit-Remaining, X-RateLimit-Reset, and status properties.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've created the header function that will communicate rate limit status to clients.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your function returns an object with all four required properties.
steps.feedbackWrong: Try creating a function named addRateLimitHeaders that returns an object with the rate limit headers.

steps.title: Plan monitoring and adaptive rate limiting
steps.instruction: Inside your defineRateLimiting function, add a new function named monitorAndAdapt that takes parameters for currentHits, systemLoad, and maxCapacity, and returns an object with adjustedLimit and shouldThrottle properties.
steps.hint: Create a function that analyzes current metrics and decides whether to adjust rate limits or throttle requests.
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have a monitoring function that can analyze system metrics and return adaptive rate limiting decisions.
successCriteria: The defineRateLimiting function contains a monitorAndAdapt function that accepts three parameters and returns an object with adjustedLimit and shouldThrottle properties.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully implemented the monitoring and adaptive rate limiting function. This completes your rate limiting system design with all essential components.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your monitorAndAdapt function accepts the three specified parameters and returns an object with both adjustedLimit and shouldThrottle properties.
steps.feedbackWrong: The monitorAndAdapt function is missing or doesn't match the required structure. It should accept currentHits, systemLoad, and maxCapacity parameters, and return an object with adjustedLimit and shouldThrottle.
